coverage: Coverage is thinner before 2016: about 54 Technology members per quarter in 2011Q4–2015Q4, against about 80 from 2021. Part of the gap is real (the sector's weight in the index grew), but FMP has no balance sheets for several Technology companies acquired in 2012–2018, including BMC Software, CA Technologies, EMC, Molex, Tellabs, CSRA and Harman, and LSI and Novellus could not be matched to FMP tickers. These were mostly mature, profitable companies, so their absence may tilt the early-period results.

**Broader Technology universe.** FMP's sector labels split similar businesses inconsistently, so some companies are moved into Technology (`panel_prep.SECTOR_OVERRIDES`): the internet platforms Alphabet, Meta, Twitter, Reddit and Match (FMP: Communication Services; GICS also had them in Information Technology until 2018) and the software companies Paychex and The Trade Desk join Software, Cerner (hospital health-record software and services) joins IT Services, and Xerox joins Hardware. Payment networks and processors (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal), solar equipment makers and e-commerce companies such as Amazon stay in their FMP sectors. The reclassification added 8 companies and 263 company-quarters; the chosen models' full-sample IC was unchanged (0.087 to 0.088).
holdout_comment: The holdout picks are weaker in the test window than the walk-forward results suggest: the 3-metric picks scored 0.065–0.087 and the 4-metric picks 0.045–0.069, against walk-forward ICs of 0.087 and 0.100. All nine picks are built on the 5-year payout ratio, which led in training. The top choice ranked 1,246th in training but scored 0.138 on the test window, the highest of the leading models. The single 2021–2025 test period is dominated by one regime, which is why model size and expected performance are judged on walk-forward testing instead.
chosen_rationale: **Three metrics.** In the first run (2026-10-18) walk-forward testing favoured 3-metric models, and the two chosen models were the strongest of that size. After the reclassification, the ROIC averages and the payout family rule, 4-metric picks lead (out-of-sample IC 0.100 against 0.087 for 3 metrics, Section 9.4), but the gap is not significant (paired t 0.56 over 35 test quarters). Most of it comes from folds 1–2, where the payout family rule removed the 4-metric picks that paired payout yield with the payout ratio (Section 9.2); from fold 3 on the 4-metric picks are unchanged. The chosen 3-metric models are therefore kept.

**Against the leading 4-metric model.** FCF_MGN_3Yr + Payout_Ratio_5Yr | Payout_CAGR_3Yr + ~CapX_Intensity_3Yr (4A, picked in every walk-forward fold from fold 3) has a slightly higher full-sample IC than the top choice (0.095 against 0.087; paired t 0.37). Its edge is all in 2011–2015 (0.099 against 0.027); the top choice is ahead by 0.052 in 2021–2025 and roughly doubles its holdout test IC (0.138 against 0.069). Their quarterly ICs are only 0.33 correlated, so 4A is a candidate to blend with rather than a replacement.

**Statistically strong.** Full-sample t-stats of 4.7 and 4.4 (adjusted t 2.0 and 1.4 after allowing for the number of models searched). On the current data they rank 7th and 20th among eligible 3-metric models by full-sample t. The six ranked above them are built on the 5-year payout ratio and lead by margins well within noise (paired t of the IC difference 0.3–0.8), and each has a lower 2021–2025 IC than the top choice.

**Positive in every era.** IC is positive in every era (0.027 in 2011–2015, 0.093 in 2016–2020, 0.137 in 2021–2025), including 2011–2015, when profitability metrics such as ROE and ROIC predicted in reverse; it is weakest in that era.

**Reliable inputs.** All three metrics are cash-flow based (free cash flow payout, cash-flow growth, capex relative to operating cash flow), which depend less on accounting choices and are more comparable across companies than earnings-based measures.
**Smoothed capex.** The 3-year capex intensity averages out one-off spending years; it raised the t of the otherwise identical 1-year version from 4.08 to 4.70.
chosen_notes: **Top vs second choice.** The two are statistically level and share two of three metrics, so they rank companies similarly. The top choice uses operating cash-flow growth, which keeps growth separate from investment; the second uses free-cash-flow growth, which already subtracts capex, so capex enters the second model twice. The second choice has the milder worst year and the clearest gain over its 2-metric parts.

**A diversifying alternative.** FCF_Payout_Ratio | CFOPS_CAGR_3Yr + Asset_G_Rate_5Yr (low 5-year total-asset growth, the Fama-French direction) is slightly stronger than the chosen pair in 2011–2015 (0.034) and has the mildest worst four-quarter stretch (−0.066 against −0.126 and −0.097), but a weaker adjusted t (0.0). It could serve as a check that behaves differently from the chosen pair.

**Alphabet and Meta.** The top choice scores both well, mainly through high capex relative to operating cash flow. Without their rows its IC would be 0.124 rather than 0.137 in 2021–2025, and 0.039 rather than 0.027 in 2011–2015: they add volatility, not average IC.
limitations: **Regime dependence.** Profitability metrics reversed in 2011–2015 and asset growth changed sign after 2015. The chosen models were stable across eras, but there is no guarantee the next regime will behave like the past ones. Part of the top choice's recent strength comes from rewarding the heavy data-centre capex of Alphabet and Meta.
**Early coverage.** Several acquired Technology companies are missing before 2016 (Section 3.6).

addon_notes: **No add-on is kept.** The best gains (reversed earnings yield at half weight, +0.023 IC, paired t 2.04; reversed earnings yield with 1-month momentum, +0.026, paired t 1.53) are about what the best of over a thousand tries produces by chance, and every adjusted t is zero. Choosing an add-on fold by fold barely changed out-of-sample IC (+0.002, paired t 0.15), and the folds picked different add-ons, a sign of noise.

**Value works in reverse in Technology.** Every add-on that helped favors more expensive stocks; cheap stocks in the conventional direction hurt, consistent with low valuations marking declining businesses in this sector. Reversed earnings yield's best bucket is a mix of very high P/E companies (median P/E about 60) and loss-makers (about a quarter of it), because earnings yield is negative for losses. Momentum adds little: 1-month returns continue weakly (single-metric IC +0.022, not significant) and 1-month reversal hurts; 3- to 24-month returns are weakly negative.
**Watch list.** Reversed earnings yield with 1-month momentum at half weight improved IC in all three eras and on the holdout, and is the add-on to re-test as more quarters accumulate.
